title: The wire
description: Every message that travels between the controller, the bus, the runner and the API, in one document because they share a vocabulary: the run and task states, the identifiers, the digests and the idempotency key are the same strings everywhere, and a $ref may not leave a document here, so an enumeration written twice would be an enumeration that drifts. There is no message at the root: a reader validates against the member it is holding, $defs/taskMessage or $defs/taskResult and so on, and the fixture index names one group per member for that reason. Nothing here is a business payload. A task message names the secrets a step mounts and carries no value, names its inputs by digest and carries no URL that works on its own, and the objects are closed so that neither can be written at all rather than merely being undocumented.

taskMessage.title: Task message
taskMessage.description: One unit of work, published by the controller on the task bus and consumed by exactly one runner. It names everything the runner needs to create a container and nothing else: the run and the step it belongs to, the image resolved to a digest, the parameters with the secret material taken out, the secrets by name and mount point, the inputs by port and digest, the ports the container may write, the ceilings, the network posture, the labels the queue was chosen by, the instant it must be stopped by, and the grant. It carries no business payload, no secret value and no URL that would work without the grant, and the object is closed so that none of those can be written here at all: unexpressible rather than merely undocumented, because a queue holds messages and a message that could carry a value eventually would. Delivery is at least once, so it is built to be replayed: the idempotency key names one attempt at one unit of work, and a runner refuses to start a container for a key that has already completed.

task_id.description: Names this task. It is what the result and the runner hooks call it, and what a pre_task hook receives as AGK_TASK_ID. It is not the idempotency key: the key names the unit of work and stays the same across every redelivery of it, while this names the task the controller created and is the handle everything else speaks about.

idempotency_key.description: What names this attempt at this unit of work, run_id/step/attempt/shard. The bus delivers at least once, so two deliveries of one message have to become one container: the runner keys its own record on this string and refuses to start for a key that has already completed. It restates what task_id, step, attempt and shard already carry, and it travels all the same because it is the one string the heartbeat lists and the result is matched on, so neither has to rebuild it and risk rebuilding it differently.

run_id.description: The run this task belongs to, and what the container reads as AGK_RUN_ID. It ties the task to the run's state, to its logs and to the artifact URIs whose first path segment is this same value, which is how a result coming back from a machine that holds no graph is filed against the right run.

namespace.description: The namespace that owns the run, which the container reads as AGK_NAMESPACE. A runner policy can restrict a host to a list of namespaces, so this is read when the task is accepted and not only after it has run, and it is what scopes the quota, the grant and every artifact the task writes.

workflow.description: The workflow and the commit the run was started from, written name@commit. The namespace travels beside it rather than inside it, since the message already names the namespace and joining the two is the reader's business. The commit is here because the runner fetches the repository tree at it and mounts that tree read only at /agk/repo: a runner never speaks git and holds no credential for it, so what it is told is a commit and it fetches content-addressed objects with the task's grant, exactly as it fetches an artifact.

step.description: The step this task runs, under the identifier the workflow gave it, which the container reads as AGK_STEP. A runner never sees the graph the step came from, so the name travels with the work rather than being looked up.

attempt.description: Which attempt this is, counting from 1. A retry publishes a new task with the same run, step and shard and a higher number, so the attempt is what keeps the envelope that was kept apart from the ones that failed before it, and it is one segment of the idempotency key. The container reads it as AGK_ATTEMPT.

shard.description: Which container of a fan-out this is, absent when the step is not fanned out. The absence is the signal: it is how the runner tells one container of eight from the only container there is, and it is why the idempotency key has three segments in one case and four in the other. The container reads it as AGK_SHARD, written index/of.

image.description: The image the container is created from, always resolved to a digest. A mutable tag is accepted in a workflow under development and is resolved once for the whole run, so what reaches a runner is never a tag: the runner pulls exactly what was decided, verifies the signature where the namespace policy requires it, and two tasks of one run cannot end up on two different builds because a tag moved between them.

params.description: The step's parameters, resolved and with the secret material taken out. A parameter the brick manifest marks sensitive is not written here at all: its value is obtained by redeeming the grant at the last moment, which is what keeps a secret off a queue that holds messages until somebody consumes them. The names are written on the parameter grammar, narrower than the rest of the workflow file because a parameter is exported to a script as AGK_PARAM_<NAME>. The values are the brick's own business, already validated against the manifest schema before the task was published, so no shape is imposed on them here and an empty object is what a step with no parameters sends.

secrets.description: The secrets the step mounts, each one a name and a mount point and never a value. The entry is closed, so a value has no key to be written under and a message carrying one is refused rather than tolerated and ignored: the controller names which secret a task may have and never reads one, the API is the only component that reads the store, and the runner obtains the value by redeeming the grant once it is about to start the container. Empty is the ordinary case and is what a step declaring no secret sends.

items.title: Mounted secret
items.description: One secret the container will be given: the name the namespace knows it by, and the path the value is mounted at. Nothing else, because nothing else can be said about a secret without saying the secret.

name.description: The secret's name, as the workflow secrets block names it and as the brick manifest asks for it. Only secrets the owning namespace declares can be named, and this is what the runner presents when it redeems the grant, so the name is the whole of what the message says about the secret.

mount.description: Where the value is mounted inside the container, on tmpfs under /agk/secrets/ and nowhere else: a mount at /run/secrets/bearer, written out of habit, is refused. It is a file and not an environment variable because a process environment is readable by its children and ends up in diagnostic dumps. The controller resolves the path before publishing, from the brick manifest or from the name, so the runner is told where to put the value rather than deriving it and deriving it differently.

inputs.description: The input envelopes the container will be given, one entry per port, named by port, digest and item count. The URLs come from redeeming the grant, and the entry is closed so that one cannot be written here at all: that is what makes a copy of the message worth nothing on its own. Reading the page took a decision worth naming: the message it prints carries a port, a digest and a count and no URL, and says the grant is redeemed for input URLs, while the task bus chapter describes the message as naming "the URIs the runner must fetch". That sentence is read here as the names the grant is redeemed against. The digests are also one of the three parts of the memoisation key, with the image digest and the resolved parameters, so a step whose inputs have not changed can be answered without being run. Empty is what a step fed by nothing upstream sends.

items.title: Input port
items.description: One envelope the container will receive, on one port. It says which port, which bytes and how many items, which is everything the runner needs to fetch it, check it and size the working directory for it.

port.description: The port the envelope arrives on, under the name the step's needs or inputs block gave it. The container finds it as a directory under /agk/in/<port>/, which is why the name carries no path separator and no space.

digest.description: The digest of the envelope that will be fetched. The runner checks what it downloaded against it, and the controller can name the same batch again on a replay without having kept a copy anywhere the runner could reach.

items.description: How many items the envelope holds. It travels so that the runner can size what it is about to fetch before fetching it, and so that a message stays readable to a component that holds no permission over the payload: the count is metadata, the contents are behind run:read_data. Zero is legitimate and is what a port fed by a skipped step carries.

outputs.description: The output ports the container may write, which is exactly what it reads as the comma separated AGK_OUT_PORTS. The list is the workflow's word rather than the image's, because a step running a script has no manifest to infer ports from and has to declare them, and the runner publishes an empty envelope for a declared port the container never wrote. A name appears once: it is a directory, a file name under /agk/out/ports/ and one entry of a comma separated list, and a repeated name would be one file described twice. An empty list is legitimate, since a step that writes nothing and exits 0 is a legitimate step.

resources.description: The ceilings the container is created with, as the manifest and the step wrote them and the runner policy and the namespace quota capped them. They travel because the runner is the one that applies them: memory becomes Memory, cpu becomes NanoCPUs and pids becomes PidsLimit. A ceiling the controller did not decide is absent rather than guessed at, and the runner falls back to its own policy, where the process ceiling defaults to 256.

network.description: What the container may reach, and always written, including for the default none: a runner reading an absent field would be deciding something the controller had already decided. Every task gets its own network, so two containers on one host never see each other, and a posture the runner cannot provide is refused rather than approximated.

egress_allow.description: The host and port pairs the runner's egress proxy will allow, exactly as the step's egress.allow block wrote them. Egress is decided per step and is default deny because it is the only control that actually bites: a brick that legitimately receives an API key can also send it elsewhere, and the proxy is what decides where. It is meaningful only under network: egress, where a runner with no proxy refuses the task rather than opening the network and calling it filtered.

runs_on.description: The label selectors the step was published under, which is what decided the queue this message went onto. They travel so that the runner can check the task against what it actually claims, which is worth something because labels are not self asserted: a runner may only ever claim the labels its join token allowed, so a machine cannot add zone=lan to itself and start receiving the steps that were kept off the internet. An empty list is a step that named no pool and is content with whichever runner the namespace is allowed to use.

deadline.description: The instant past which the container is stopped, which it reads as AGK_DEADLINE. It is an instant and not the duration the step's timeout was written as, for the reason the shared timestamp records: two machines disagreeing about how long is left is worse than two machines disagreeing about what time it is. On expiry the container gets SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a grace period the runner policy sets; no keyword of the workflow file sets that grace, so it is not on the wire either.

grant.description: The bearer token issued with this task, and the only thing that turns the names in this message into values. The runner redeems it at the API for the input URLs, the URLs of the workflow tree, the secret values and the upload URLs, and for nothing that belongs to another task: it is scoped to this one and expires with it. It is the hinge the whole message turns on, since everything else here is a name, and a name without this token names what was going to happen and grants none of it.

script.description: The commands the container runs, where the step named a base image rather than a brick. A list and never one block of text, because "the list is what makes that exit attributable to one command rather than to a script". It is the workflow author's own words rather than business data: a task message carries no payload, and a command somebody wrote in agentiik.yaml is not one.

before_script.description: Commands run in the same container before script, for setting up what script assumes. A non-zero exit here fails the step before script runs at all.

after_script.description: Commands run in the same container after script, and run even when script failed, so that a diagnostic dump survives a failure. Its own exit code does not change the step's verdict, which is the runner's to keep true because it is the runner that watches the two and reports one.

shell.description: The interpreter the commands are handed to, as an argument vector. It travels because the image is the workflow's choice and the interpreter inside it is not something a runner may assume: a distroless base has no shell at all.

from.description: The path or glob in the repository tree, at the run's commit.

to.description: Where it is mounted in the container, an absolute path. Absent where the step asked for no relocation, as the short form of a selector never does: the file is then where it is under /agk/repo/.

mode.description: The mode the file is created with, where the step asked for one.

items.description: One file of the repository tree, and where the container sees it.

files.description: The repository files this step asked for, named by where they are and where they go. The bytes are not here: they are fetched from the tree by redeeming the grant, exactly as an input is, which is what keeps a copy of this message worth nothing on its own.

timeout.description: How long this shard may take, as the step declared it. It travels beside deadline rather than instead of it because the two answer different questions: the deadline is the instant this attempt is stopped at, and the timeout is what a person reading the message sees the workflow having asked for.

idempotent.description: Whether running this again on the same inputs is safe, which is what decides whether a lost task may be requeued and whether its result may be cached. It travels because the runner is what refuses to start a container for a key that has already completed, and because "a lost task is charged to the infrastructure and is requeued only when the step is declared idempotent".

cache_key.description: The memoisation key, where the step asked to be cached. It "combines the image digest, the resolved parameters and the digests of the input envelopes, prefixed by the namespace, and it never crosses a namespace boundary", which is why it is computed by the controller and carried rather than worked out by whoever holds the task.

taskResult.title: Task result
taskResult.description: What a runner publishes when a task ends, and the only message the controller reads to decide what happens next: whether the step is done, whether it is retried, what the next tasks are handed and what the run detail shows. It names the task twice, by dispatch and by idempotency key, and repeats nothing the key already spells, so the run, the step, the attempt and the shard have one source on the wire rather than two that can disagree. It carries no item and no artifact content: what travels is a digest per port and a digest per artifact, which is what lets the controller schedule on metadata while the payload stays behind run:read_data. The fields that describe a container are present exactly where a container ran, and the state says which case this is: succeeded and failed report an exit code and a span, lost reports neither, because the point of lost is that there is no outcome to report. The bus delivers at least once, so the controller has to read a redelivered result as the same result; nothing here is a counter it could add twice.

allOf.$comment: A container that ran under a state that reports an outcome exited, and an exit is a code and an instant. With the dependentRequired above, exit_code and started_at imply each other in those two states, which is the whole of the rule that an exit code exists where a container ran and does not where none did.

Success is exit code 0 and nothing else, because the exit code table reads the verdict off that number alone. A succeeded task also writes its ports, empty list included, so that the controller can tell a step that published nothing from a runner that said nothing.

A lost task has no outcome at all, so every field that would describe one is refused rather than left optional. A result claiming lost and a finished_at at once is the result the controller cannot read: it would say both that nothing observed the end and when the end was.

task_id.description: The dispatch this result answers, carried back unchanged from the task message. A requeue after loss keeps the idempotency key and takes a new task_id, so this is what tells two deliveries of one unit of work apart in the audit log, where the key deliberately cannot.

idempotency_key.description: The unit of work this result belongs to, and what the controller matches it against. It matches on this rather than on task_id because the bus delivers at least once and a requeued task carries a new dispatch identifier for the same work: matching on the key is what makes a second delivery a no-op instead of a second completion.

runner.title: Runner
runner.description: The runner that produced the result, under the name it joined with. It travels because the controller has to charge an infrastructure failure to a host, drain that host and show the run detail where the work actually ran, none of which the idempotency key says. The documentation prints a name and does not fix its grammar, so the schema takes the lowercase hyphenated form it prints, which is how every other name on the wire is written; a looser field would let one host appear under two spellings.

state.description: How the task ended, which is one of the five endings and never a state it passed through: a heartbeat is what says a task is still running, and a result saying so would be a result for work that has not finished. succeeded and failed come from the container's own exit; lost is declared by the controller rather than reported here, and travels on a result only where a runner recovers one it had already lost; timed_out and cancelled are the runner stopping the container, the first at the step's deadline and the second because the run was cancelled.

exit_code.title: Exit code
exit_code.description: The status the container exited with, present wherever one ran. Nothing else declares the verdict: 0 is success, 1 to 99 is an application failure retried only where retry.on says so, 100 to 119 is transient and retried by the step policy, 120 is never retried whatever retry says, 121 to 124 are reserved for the runner, and 125 and above is read as infrastructure and charged to the runner rather than to the brick. The ceiling is 255 and not 124 because a container stopped at its deadline reports 128 plus the signal, so 137 is an ordinary value here and not an eighth band.

started_at.description: When the container started, on the runner's clock. It bounds what usage measures, together with finished_at, and that is also why the image pull is reported separately: the pull happens before this instant, and counting it here would charge the brick for a download.

finished_at.description: When the container exited. A lost task has none of its own, because nothing observed the end: the controller knows only when it stopped hearing, and that instant belongs to its record rather than to a runner that cannot claim it. Present wherever there is an exit code, absent wherever there is not.

outputs.title: Published ports
outputs.description: One entry per declared output port, naming the envelope published on it. Every declared port appears, including the ones the container never wrote, because an unwritten port publishes an empty envelope and an empty envelope has a digest like any other. A failed task may carry ports too: the documentation's own result example is a failed task publishing two of them, which is how a brick separates the items it rejected from the run failing whole. uniqueItems refuses the same entry twice; that two entries name one port with different digests is a thing the controller refuses, not a shape this schema can describe.

port.description: The output port the envelope left by, under the name the brick declares. The names are the brick's own, so no set of values is fixed here.

digest.description: The digest of the serialised envelope this task produced on that port. Where the step is fanned out the shard envelopes are concatenated port by port before publication, so it is the concatenation and not this digest that reaches the next task message as an input digest. The controller never opens the batch either way, which is what keeps scheduling out of the payload.

items.title: Item count
items.description: How many items the envelope holds, the same number its meta.count carries. It travels here so that a condition written on inputs.<port>.count can be weighed without the envelope being read, and so that the run detail can show an empty port as empty rather than as unknown.

artifacts.title: Written artifacts
artifacts.description: What the task wrote to the object store, by digest and by size. The controller records one reference per entry, and a reference is what expiry drops: the physical object is collected when its count reaches zero, so a result that did not list what it wrote would leave bytes nobody is counting. An entry is reported even where the store already held those bytes, because what is declared is the reference and not the write, and deduplication is exactly the case where the two differ.

sha256.title: Artifact digest
sha256.description: The digest of the artifact's bytes, sixty four lowercase hexadecimal characters, which is also the <digest> the physical key sha256/<digest> is built from. The key names the algorithm, so the value does not repeat it, exactly as an envelope writes a file's digest; the prefixed form belongs where the field is called digest. The documentation elides the middle of a digest for the page, and that elision is typography rather than a value.

bytes.title: Size
bytes.description: How many bytes the artifact holds. It is what the run detail keeps showing beside the digest once the artifact has expired or been collected, and what a namespace's storage is counted against. An envelope calls the same measure size on a file entry: each field keeps the name its own message gives it rather than being tidied into one.

log.title: Captured log
log.description: Where the task's output went, how much of it there is and whether it was cut. The runner captures the container's standard error, timestamps it, indexes it and caps it. Ports travel as files under /agk/out/ports/, which is what keeps standard output usable for diagnostics, and a script that writes no port and exits 0 has its standard output published as the single out port. A task that never reached a container writes what stopped it to the same place, a refused pull or a grant that would not redeem being the usual reasons, so this does not depend on a container having run and is the only thing such a result has to say for itself.

uri.title: Log URI
uri.description: Where the log is addressed from. The scheme names a kind in its first segment and a log is its own: agk://log/<run>/<task>, not the agk://run/ space an artifact is addressed in. A log belongs to one task and not to one port, which is why it cannot be addressed like an artifact: a step fanned out into eight shards has eight logs and no port to tell them apart, and a task identifier tells them apart exactly. The task carries slashes of its own, so it is escaped as a path segment.

lines.title: Lines
lines.description: How many lines were captured. It is a count of lines rather than of bytes because that is the unit the log is indexed in, and it is on the result so that the console can show the size of what it is about to fetch.

truncated.title: Truncated
truncated.description: Whether the cap was reached and the rest of the output dropped. It is its own field because the count cannot say it: four hundred lines is either the whole log or the first four hundred of one, and somebody chasing a failure has to know which before reading the last line as the last thing that happened.

usage.title: Usage
usage.description: What the container actually consumed, measured by the runner because nothing else can see it and reported here because the container is gone by the time anyone asks. It is what an author reads before changing resources, and what an operator reads when a ceiling turns out to be the thing that failed. The three figures come from one read of the container's statistics, so a result carrying a usage block carries all three: two numbers and a gap is a number nobody can compare.

cpu_seconds.title: CPU seconds
cpu_seconds.description: CPU time consumed, in seconds. It is not the wall clock span between started_at and finished_at, and the two differ by however oversubscribed the host was, which is the difference an author has to see before blaming the brick for a slow step.

max_rss_bytes.title: Peak resident set
max_rss_bytes.description: The largest resident set the container reached, in bytes. It says how close the memory ceiling was, which is the number to raise or lower resources.memory against rather than guessing; a task the kernel killed for memory reports a figure at its ceiling and not the one it was reaching for, and the exit code is what says that is what happened.

image_pull_ms.title: Image pull
image_pull_ms.description: How long the image pull took, in milliseconds, and 0 where the host already held it. An image is cached by digest, so the first task to need it on a host pays for the pull and the rest do not: reporting it separately keeps that cost out of the container's span instead of hiding it inside a step's duration and making one host look slow.

runnerRegistration.title: Runner registration
runnerRegistration.description: The one exchange that turns a machine nobody has met into a runner of a named pool: what the agent sends the API at join, and what the API answers. Both halves are written as one subschema because neither is legible alone: the request proves which pool the machine belongs to and says what it is, and the answer is the only place that machine ever learns its own identity and receives a credential. It happens once. Everything after it, heartbeats, grant redemptions, log shipping, is the runner reaching out holding what this answer carried, which is why nothing here is sent again on a later call.

request.title: Join request
request.description: What the runner sends, over HTTPS and outbound, in the one call it makes before it holds a credential. It is authenticated by the join token in its body and by nothing else, because the machine has nothing else yet. The object is closed and carries no private key, no address and no pool: the private half of the keypair never leaves the host, nothing ever connects inbound to a runner so an address would be a field no component could use, and the pool travels in the token rather than being claimed, so that a machine cannot join a pool by naming it.

token.title: Join token
token.description: The join token an administrator issued, and which this call spends. It is single use, so a second registration presenting it is refused rather than producing a second runner, and short lived, one hour by default, so a token that leaks has usually expired before anyone reaches it. It is bound to one pool and to the exact set of labels the runner may claim, which is why neither of those is claimed here. The prefix says which door the value belongs at, so it can be refused early and recognised in a log that should not be holding it, and the pattern refuses anything shorter than forty-three characters after it, which is the shortest base64url that can hold the 256 bits of entropy every token, join token and grant in this installation carries; the longer spellings hexadecimal and base32 produce are accepted too. The API keeps only the hash.

public_key.title: Public key
public_key.description: The public half of the keypair the agent generated on this host, written as PEM around a SubjectPublicKeyInfo. The private half never leaves the machine and has no field here: the object is closed, so a request that carried one would be refused rather than accepted and quietly ignored. This key is the runner's identity across restarts, which is what makes a reimaged host a new runner that joins again instead of a record silently reused. The encoding is chosen because it names the algorithm inside the value, so no second field has to agree on it out of band, and because the standard library writes it without a dependency.
